account: A 50-year-old woman who had recently had COVID-19 had dyspnea. Four days before admission, a primary care physician measured her oxygen saturation at 94 to 98 percent, and her chest radiograph and electrocardiogram were normal. She was referred to the authors' hospital (Oita University, Yufu, Japan) for assessment of dyspnea. Hospital pulse oximetry read 97%, but her Apple Watch Series 7 had shown an oxygen saturation of 88% in the early morning. Prompted by the watch reading, clinicians did emergent computed tomography angiography. It showed filling defects in multiple pulmonary artery branches, which confirmed pulmonary embolism with bilateral deep venous thrombosis. She was treated with a direct oral anticoagulant. Oxygen was stopped on day 6, and she was discharged on day 15. The authors state that the watch's low reading led to the diagnosis. They write that it might have been hard to think of pulmonary embolism without the watch data. The case appeared online in QJM on 5 September 2022, and the report does not give the date of the event. A systematic review published on 23 February 2023 by authors at Kantonsspital Winterthur and Inselspital Bern covered five studies of the Series 6 with 973 patients. The review's authors found that the watch shows no strong systematic bias against medical-grade pulse oximeters and that outliers of up to 15 points occur.

ai_role.statement: The watch's pulse-oximetry algorithm recorded the 88% reading in the early morning. Spot oximetry at primary care and at the hospital had been normal. The authors write that it might have been hard to think of pulmonary embolism without the watch data, and clinicians made the diagnosis with CT angiography. The letter describes no automatic alert and does not say who reported the reading.

Hospital pulse oximetry read 97%, but her Apple Watch Series 7 had shown an oxygen saturation of 88% in the early morning. Prompted by the watch reading, clinicians did emergent computed tomography angiography. It showed filling defects in multiple pulmonary artery branches, which confirmed pulmonary embolism with bilateral deep venous thrombosis. She was treated with a direct oral anticoagulant. Oxygen was stopped on day 6, and she was discharged on day 15. The authors state that the watch's low reading led to the diagnosis. They write that it might have been hard to think of pulmonary embolism without the watch data. The case appeared online in QJM on 5 September 2022, and the report does not give the date of the event. A systematic review published on 23 February 2023 by authors at Kantonsspital Winterthur and Inselspital Bern covered five studies of the Series 6 with 973 patients. The review's authors found that the watch shows no strong systematic bias against medical-grade pulse oximeters and that outliers of up to 15 points occur.

summary: The Blood Oxygen app on an Apple Watch Series 7 recorded an oxygen saturation of 88%, which led clinicians in Japan to computed tomography angiography that found a pulmonary embolism.
title: Apple Watch Blood Oxygen reading leading to diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary embolism
